key_terms.meaning: A type such as uint8_t or int16_t from stdint.h whose bit width is guaranteed the same on every compiler, unlike plain int.
A type qualifier saying the object can change outside the program's control, so the compiler must perform a real load or store at every access and never cache it in a register.
A constant whose set bits choose the register bits you want to read, set or clear, for example 0x04 selects bit 2.
A C function with no arguments and no return value that the hardware calls when its interrupt fires; it should be short and must clear the interrupt source.
A compiler that runs on the host machine (your PC) and emits machine code for a different target processor.
A file that tells the linker which sections (.text, .data, .bss, heap, stack) go at which physical addresses in target memory.
The small routine that runs before main: sets the stack pointer, copies initialised data from flash to RAM, clears .bss and jumps to main.
A serial test and debug port using TCK, TMS, TDI and TDO (TRST optional) that shifts data through a scan chain inside the chip.
A host program that models the target processor instruction by instruction, giving full visibility of registers and memory without any real board.
Hardware that imitates the target chip and connects to its socket or debug port, giving real-time execution plus breakpoints and register trace.
The staged process of requirement, design, implementation, integration, testing and maintenance, with a review check before each stage is closed.
Deciding early, and jointly, which system functions become custom hardware and which run as software on a processor.
The calendar time from product concept to first saleable unit; late delivery loses revenue even if the product is technically better.
A shift-register cell placed behind every device pin; in test mode it can drive the pin or capture its logic level.
The boundary-scan instruction that connects pin cells to the external nets so that board-level interconnect and solder joints can be tested.
P = α·C·V²·f, where α is switching activity, C the switched capacitance in farads, V the supply voltage in volts and f the clock frequency in hertz.
Dynamic voltage and frequency scaling: lowering supply voltage and clock together, cutting dynamic power roughly as the square of the voltage drop.
Stopping the clock to an idle block so its flip-flops do not switch, which removes that block's dynamic power.
Switching off the supply to a block with a transistor in series, which removes its leakage current as well as its dynamic power.
A low-power processor state where the core clock is stopped and only a chosen wake-up source, such as a timer or an external interrupt pin, stays alive.

takeaways: Embedded C differs from desktop C mainly in discipline: fixed-width types, volatile on every hardware register, masks instead of bit-fields, and short interrupt routines.
A cross-toolchain is compiler plus assembler plus linker plus libraries, and the linker script and startup code are as important as the C source because they place code in physical memory.
Simulators are cheap and fully visible but slow and unrealistic; emulators and in-circuit debuggers are realistic but costly, so real projects use both at different stages.
The EDLC puts a review gate between stages, which catches interface and timing mistakes before they become expensive board re-spins.
Co-design exists because the hardware-software split fixes cost, power and schedule early; changing it late throws away most of the design.
Automotive and driver-assistance systems add hard real-time deadlines and safety requirements, so their software is tested at unit, integration and system level.
FPGAs give true parallel hardware with deterministic timing, while GPUs give high throughput for regular data-parallel work at the cost of higher power and programming effort.
Boundary scan tests the board, not the program: it finds open and short nets and missing solder without a bed-of-nails fixture.
Low-power design attacks both terms of the power budget: dynamic power through voltage, frequency and clock gating, and static power through power gating and sleep states.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to move from the tool or technique to its place in the development flow, then to a concrete case study with numbers, timing constraints or test steps, so label your diagrams and state assumptions about memory map and clock speed.

bank.q: Explain why the volatile qualifier is compulsory for memory-mapped hardware registers in Embedded C, and describe what a compiler may wrongly do if it is omitted.
outline: Memory-mapped register address defined as a pointer to volatile
Compiler may keep the value in a register and skip repeated reads
Example: polling a status flag in a while loop never exits
volatile forces a load on each access and a store on each write
Also mention fixed-width types and masks for portability

bank.q: Describe the stages a C source file passes through in a cross-toolchain until a target executable image is produced, naming the linker script and startup code.
outline: Host versus target distinction
Preprocessor, compiler, assembler, linker, objcopy to hex or binary
Runtime library and startup code linked in first
Linker script fixes section addresses to the target memory map
Symbol table retained in ELF for the debugger
Download to flash through programmer or debug probe

bank.q: Compare a simulator, an in-circuit emulator and an in-circuit debugger on realism, visibility of internal state, cost and the development stage where each is best used.
outline: Simulator: host model, full visibility, no timing realism, zero hardware cost, used in early unit testing
Emulator: mimics the chip, real-time, expensive, used in integration
In-circuit debugger over JTAG: runs on the real board, breakpoints and memory access, cheap, some intrusion
Table of comparison on four criteria
Statement of when to switch from one to the next

bank.q: List the stages of the embedded development life cycle and state the deliverable and review check produced at each stage.
outline: Requirement analysis: functional and non-functional specification
Design: architecture, hardware-software partition
Implementation: coding and unit testing
Integration: modules and hardware brought together
Testing and validation against requirements
Maintenance and field support
Configuration management and review gate at each stage

bank.q: Define area, speed, power, flexibility and time-to-market as figures of merit for a co-design decision, and give one example of a trade between any two of them.
outline: Area: gate count or die area in mm²
Speed: throughput and worst-case latency
Power: dynamic and leakage, in mW
Flexibility: ease of changing function after fabrication
Time-to-market: calendar time to first sale
Trade example: custom hardware is faster and lower power but less flexible and slower to design

bank.q: Write Embedded C for an 8-bit port register at address 0x400F0000 to set bit 2, clear bit 5 and toggle bit 0 without disturbing the other bits, and explain the read-modify-write hazard.
outline: Pointer definition with volatile and fixed-width type
Mask constants for bits 0, 2 and 5
Set: register |= mask; clear: register &= ~mask; toggle: register ^= mask
Why read-modify-write can lose an update if an ISR touches the same register
Fix by disabling interrupts or using an atomic set/clear register
Comment on write-one-to-clear flags

bank.q: Given a target with 256 kB flash starting at 0x00000000 and 64 kB RAM starting at 0x20000000, describe the contents of the linker script and the work done by the startup code.
outline: MEMORY block declaring flash and RAM origin and length
SECTIONS block placing .text and .rodata in flash, .data with load address in flash and run address in RAM, .bss in RAM
Heap and stack placement and stack size check
Startup: set stack pointer, copy .data, zero .bss, call main
Vector table at the start of flash
Linker map file used to verify

bank.q: A two-chip net on an assembled board must be checked for an open solder joint. Describe a boundary-scan sequence using IDCODE, EXTEST, SAMPLE, BYPASS and the four TAP signals.
outline: TAP states and the five signals TCK, TMS, TDI, TDO, TRST
Reset, read IDCODE on both devices
Load BYPASS on the far device to shorten the chain
Load EXTEST on the driving device, drive a known pattern on the pin
Load SAMPLE on the receiving device, shift out and compare
Open or short conclusion; mention SAMPLE for non-intrusive monitoring

bank.q: A microcontroller runs at 3.3 V and 48 MHz. DVFS lowers it to 1.8 V and 24 MHz. Compute the change in dynamic power and comment on leakage and on real-time performance.
outline: P = α·C·V²·f, α and C assumed constant
Voltage ratio 1.8/3.3 = 0.545, squared = 0.297
Frequency ratio 0.5
New dynamic power ≈ 0.149 of the old, about 85% saving
Leakage falls with voltage but is not zero; sleep modes still needed
Deadline check: worst-case execution time roughly doubles

bank.q: A battery-powered sensor node must run ten years on one cell. Analyse how co-design choices, clock and power gating, and sleep modes together decide the energy budget, and where a custom hardware block helps.
outline: Energy per wake-up = power × time, summed over active and sleep periods
Duty cycling: radio and processor active for a few milliseconds only
Co-design: put repeated filtering in hardware so the core stays asleep
Clock gating inside the active window, power gating between windows
Sleep current dominates the budget; leakage and regulator quiescent current matter
Trade: extra hardware area and design time against battery life

bank.q: Compare an FPGA, a GPU and a fast microcontroller as the computing platform for a compute-heavy embedded task such as real-time image filtering. Judge on throughput, latency, power, cost and design effort.
outline: FPGA: spatial parallelism, deterministic latency, low power per operation, harder design in HDL, high unit cost at low volume
GPU: high throughput on regular data-parallel loops, high power, deep software stack, poor for hard real-time
Fast MCU or DSP: cheapest, easiest, limited throughput
Metric: operations per second per watt
Decision depends on volume, latency guarantee and team skill
Mention hybrid SoC with CPU plus FPGA fabric

bank.q: An automotive driver-assistance function must brake within a fixed deadline and must not fail dangerously. Evaluate how the EDLC stages, in-circuit debugging and board-level testing combine to give confidence in the product.
outline: Requirement stage: hard deadline, worst-case execution time budget, safety goal
Design: partition between sensor, processor and actuator; hardware-software co-design of the perception path
Implementation: MISRA-style coding rules, static analysis, unit tests
Integration and testing: hardware-in-the-loop, fault injection, boundary scan for board defects
In-circuit debug during bring-up, removed or locked in production
Maintenance: field data, over-the-air update policy, traceability of every change

bank.q: Explain why an ISR must be short, how deferred processing is arranged, and how the choice of sleep mode interacts with interrupt latency in a real-time system.
outline: ISR blocks lower-priority interrupts and delays other work
Long ISRs cause missed deadlines and jitter
Deferred processing: set a flag or queue an item, do the work in the main loop or a task
Nested interrupts and priority assignment
Deeper sleep modes wake more slowly, adding latency
Measure and state the wake-up time against the deadline

bank.q: Describe the TAP controller states and the role of the boundary-scan register, TCK, TMS, TDI, TDO and TRST in a scan chain of three devices.
outline: 16-state machine driven by TMS on rising edge of TCK
Shift-DR and Shift-IR paths; data through TDI to TDO
Instruction register selects EXTEST, SAMPLE, BYPASS or IDCODE
Devices daisy-chained, so the chain length equals the sum of register lengths
TRST resets the TAP asynchronously where provided
BYPASS shortens the chain to one bit per device

bank.q: Explain how you would use an in-circuit debugger over JTAG to find a firmware hang that appears only on the real board and never in the simulator.
outline: Attach debugger, halt the core, read program counter and stack
Breakpoints and watchpoints on the suspect variable
Read peripheral registers to check clock, pin mux and status flags
Compare board timing, supply and reset behaviour with simulation assumptions
Trace or single-step through the suspect path
Fix and re-test both in simulation and on the board

glossary.def: A computer built into a larger device to perform a dedicated function under real-time constraints.
A single chip containing a processor core, flash, RAM and peripherals such as timers, serial ports and converters.
A scheme where peripheral registers appear at ordinary memory addresses, so normal load and store instructions drive the hardware.
A hardware register inside a microcontroller that controls a peripheral or holds its status.
The desktop or laptop machine on which you compile and debug, as opposed to the target that runs the code.
The actual embedded processor or board for which the program is built and on which it runs.
A bit pattern used with AND, OR and XOR to change selected bits of a register and leave the rest untouched.
A counter that resets the processor if the software fails to clear it within a fixed period, recovering from hangs.
A small program that runs at reset, optionally updates the main firmware, and then jumps to the application.
A debugger setting that halts the processor when execution reaches a chosen address.
A debugger setting that halts the processor when a chosen memory location is read or written.
The 16-state machine inside a JTAG device that sequences instructions and data through the scan chain on the clock TCK.
Two or more JTAG devices daisy-chained from TDI to TDO so that one port reaches all of them.
Board test using probes or boundary-scan cells to check nets and component connections after assembly.
The longest time a code path can take on the target, used to prove a real-time deadline is met.
Testing where real controller hardware runs against a simulated plant so that timing and I/O are realistic.
System on chip: a processor, memory and several peripherals integrated on one die.
Field-programmable gate array: a chip whose logic and wiring are configured after manufacture to form custom digital circuits.
Graphics processing unit: a processor with many simple cores that executes the same instruction over large data arrays.
Power drawn by a transistor that is off, caused by sub-threshold and gate leakage currents; it grows as devices shrink.
Running a node active for a short time and asleep for the rest, so average power falls in proportion to the active fraction.
The delay between an event and the response to it, measured in microseconds or milliseconds.
Software stored in non-volatile memory on the embedded device and rarely or never changed by the user.
A published set of coding rules for C that avoids constructs with unreliable or undefined behaviour, used in safety-related embedded software.
